Patient demographics:
  age: 24
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Diplomat
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Drug Use: take drugs, Compulsive Exercise: I push myself to exercise excessively, Concealing Clothing: wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed
  Threat: Cannot Trust Safety: Even when others tell me I am safe I find it impossible to believe it, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
  Memory: Cannot Find Words: I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen, Hopelessness: I have no future

Vignette:
Arjun stood in the market square when the ground shattered beneath him, the concrete dust and burning oil clinging to his clothes. What he remembers most clearly is not a single narrative but a series of sharp, unblinking frames: the sudden impact, the man in the grey coat falling forward, the acrid bite of fuel mixing with the familiar tang of his own sweat. Even now, Arjun can close his eyes and smell it again—the same sharp, oily scent that floods his throat when the memory surfaces. He knows exactly what happened to him that afternoon, yet when a colleague tries to coax the story from him, his tongue remains heavy, unable to find words to bridge the gap between knowing and speaking. The images stay sharp, locked behind his ribs, his memories of the frightening event clear and detailed, as if the event never fully left his peripheral vision. Returning to his life as a diplomat in Washington, Arjun learned to navigate a world that felt suddenly porous. He had come to believe that safety was a promise others made lightly, and even when his fiancée assured him the streets were secure, he found it impossible to believe it. A car backfiring down K Street sent his shoulders rising before his mind could register the sound; the sharp crack carried him instantly back to the square, his body bracing as if the stressful experience were actually happening again. What frightened him most was the smell of alcohol on a stranger’s breath or the faint clink of a glass in a diplomatic lobby, which would stir that same scent from the past and tighten his chest. Strangers approaching him in ordinary moments—a courier reaching for a signature, a colleague stepping too close in an elevator—made him feel threatened, as though their proximity carried a quiet weight. He had lost faith in the steady rhythm of daily life, certain that something about him had drawn the violence down, as though his very presence had made the event inevitable. To manage the mounting pressure, Arjun developed quiet routines that became his daily architecture. He began wearing concealing clothing to avoid being noticed in crowded embassy halls and official cars, the layered wool and structured collars creating a quiet boundary around his shoulders. When the memories grew loud, he pushed himself to exercise excessively, running until his breath steadied and his mind quieted. He repeated this with a kind of mechanical insistence, lacing his shoes each morning without fail. When physical exhaustion alone could not still the noise, he began taking drugs, letting the soft chemistry wash over him until the edges of the room softened again. These habits sat side by side in his days, each offering a different kind of shelter as the months passed, without one replacing the other. Now twenty-four, Arjun works in the diplomatic corps, where his office windows face a busy thoroughfare and his schedule demands constant interaction. He feels emotionally vulnerable in the open glass corridors of the embassy, where the hum of voices and the cadence of footsteps remind him of the square. He has a future on paper, but he has lost faith in its promise. He sits in his apartment some evenings, listening to his partner laugh in the other room, yet he is certain that the ground could still give way. He knows the world is physically safe, but he cannot trust the feeling of it. What brought him to seek help was not a single breaking point, but the slow accumulation of these quiet moments: the way he now counts exits in every building, the way he flinches when a door closes too sharply, the way he watches strangers approach his desk with a guarded stillness. He hopes someone might help him untangle the knot between what he knows and what he feels, though he carries a quiet hopelessness, certain he has no future unless he can quiet the watchfulness that keeps him standing at attention.
